today.name: Caldera

With 0.5 you can plant notes in a Garden folder and each one becomes a page, and [[@handle/Note]] links connect gardens with backlinks on both sides. today.name: Unfenced
today.tagline: Land for sale that actually borders public land
today.description: Checks ~700,000 U.S. listings every week against official public-land maps and shows the ~13,600 homes and land parcels that actually touch national forest, BLM and state land. Each one is measured from its county parcel boundary: the shared edge in feet, drawn on a map, plus how much public land is behind it, elevation, road access, flood zone and wildfire hazard. Search by ZIP or state. Free, no account needed.

comments.text: Hi Product Hunt! I'm David, and I built Unfenced. In the 1980s, my grandfather and his brother, along with a few of their friends, bought roughly 240 acres of wooded land in the northern Lower Peninsula of Michigan. It backed up to thousands of acres of state land, so the property line was never really an edge. You could walk out into the woods and just keep going. Years later I went looking for land of my own in the Poconos and wanted that same feeling. I found a parcel that borders state game lands, but getting there meant reading listings that said "near state land" and then working through county GIS maps to see whether a property actually touched the boundary or was just somewhere nearby. Unfenced does that check for about 700,000 U.S. listings, every week. It takes each property's county parcel boundary, compares it with the USGS map of public land, and shows the ones that actually touch it, with the shared boundary measured in feet and drawn on a map. Each property also shows: • how much connected public land is behind it, and who manages it • its elevation, and whether a mapped road reaches it • its FEMA flood zone and Forest Service wildfire hazard (new this week) You can search by ZIP code and distance, browse by state or by national forest, or just pan the map. It's free, with no sign-up and no cookies. I'd love feedback, especially from hunters, homesteaders and anyone who has bought rural land: what would you want to know about a property next to public land that the site doesn't tell you yet?

comments.text: We're launching the general availability of Jockey today, and it's shaped by what we learned during the research preview. We heard three things loud and clear:People needed the connectors to work better. The strongest reactions came through Claude and ChatGPT. So we prioritized ChatGPT support for GA and made the MCP experience seamless. If you want to query your library, your chat interface should be the last friction point, not the first.Builders needed output they could control. Developers told us a black-box "final edit" wasn't what they wanted. They needed structured clips, JSON, artifacts they could manipulate. So we built durable artifacts that can be saved, shared, revoked, or deleted and ensured the API gives you timestamped, actionable output you own, not a render you're stuck with.Users wanted deep social intelligence, not just basic video search. Creators and marketers kept asking us: "Why is this video trending? What specific hooks are holding attention? What common patterns make these reels go viral?" We listened, and built social intelligence features that analyze video hooks, breakdown visual and audio pacing, and explain what actually works across trending content. We also added social ingestion of URL links from YouTube, TikTok, and Instagram Reels, so users can analyze what's working in the wild and search performance alongside content without having to upload videos. It's a whole new way to deconstruct viral video performance.Library-level understanding is the point. You point Jockey at thousands of videos and images, and it reasons across all of them, not just one. That's why we built it this way, and why every model upgrade makes it better without you lifting a finger.If you're building a video app, organizing footage, or trying to find something in thousands of hours of content, Jockey is for you. Try Jockey and let us know you feedback and we will fix it!

week.name: Google EmbeddingGemma 2
week.tagline: An open, lightweight multimodal embedding model
week.description: EmbeddingGemma 2 is Google DeepMind's open embedding model that maps text, code, images, video and audio into one shared space, so you can search across them from a single query. At 740M parameters it runs on-device, needing about 567MB of RAM on a Pixel 11 Pro for the full multimodal model (191MB for text only). Apache 2.0 licensed, with weights on Hugging Face and Kaggle. MTEB Code score rises from 68.76 to 78.68.

comments.text: EmbeddingGemma 2 is Google DeepMind's open, lightweight multimodal embedding model. It maps text, code, images, video and audio into one shared space and is small enough to run on a phone.Problem: Searching by meaning usually needs a pipeline of separate models: a captioning model for images, speech-to-text for audio, a text embedder on top. That's slow, memory-hungry, and often sends your data to the cloud. For private, on-device apps, that's a hard trade-off.Solution: One 740M-parameter model, built on the Gemma 4 architecture, that embeds all five types of content in the same space. A text query can find a photo, and a voice memo can find a video clip. Everything runs locally, so your data never has to leave the device.What makes it different: It's modular. You can load only the encoders you need, as little as 270M parameters for text and code, plus optional vision (170M) and audio (300M) encoders. With quantization on a Pixel 11 Pro, it needs about 191MB of RAM for text only and about 567MB for the full multimodal model. It shares its tokenizer and audio encoder with Gemma 4, so running both together uses less memory than running them separately.Key features:Text, code, images, video and audio in a single embedding space8K token context (4x EmbeddingGemma 1), enough for about 5.5 minutes of audio, 29 images or 58 video framesVectors can be shrunk from 768 to 512, 256 or 128 dimensions for up to 6x less storageCode retrieval improves from 68.76 to 78.68 on MTEB Code (+9.92 points)Google says it leads sub-1B multimodal embedding models on benchmarks like MTEB Code and MAEB (audio)Can also act as a zero-shot, on-device decision engine: Google's MediaPipe demo scores 500 options per turn in a chess game in under 100 msWorks with transformers, sentence-transformers, MLX, vLLM, llama.cpp, SGLang, Ollama, LMStudio, Qdrant and UnslothWho it's for: Developers building private, offline-capable search, RAG, media retrieval or local codebase search, and anyone who wants cross-modal search without a cloud dependency. month.name: Rill Browser
month.tagline: The browser where Claude Code and Codex work beside you
month.description: Rill is an AI-native browser built around the Claude Code and Codex you already use. Browse normally, then press ⌘E on any page to turn what you're looking at into a task for your agent. Rill finds the right project, passes along the context, and the agent works while you keep browsing. It also sorts your tabs into themes, turns your history into days you can search, and brings every project your agents are working on into one place. Free, on the plan you already have.

comments.text: Hi Product Hunt, I'm William! I made Rill because I want to always stay in the flow. As an ADHD, I never liked code-switching. It's a browser with your Claude Code or Codex working alongside you. When something on a page gives you an idea, you say so right there, and an agent starts on it in the right project. You don't have to spend time looking for the right folder, rephrasing everything you just saw on the web, and you don't switch in and out of work mode. The work goes on with you in the flow.This matters now more than ever. Agents have shortened the distance between ideas to output near zero. So the bottleneck is capturing the idea at the moment you have it. That moment is nearly always while you're taking something in, and that is what a browser is for.Rill is a free AI-native browser. It's WebKit-based, which means it's native to Mac. Full disclosure — I'm a big fan of Anthropic and actually built an app that works exclusively with Claude Desktop for secure local file search. So I've spent a lot of time thinking about this space.My concern with Cowork isn't the vision, it's the architecture. Agentic tasks burn through tokens fast (Anthropic says so themselves), so that $200/month cap can disappear quicker than you'd expect. And at that price, you'd want to use it for real work — but the whole thing requires giving Claude direct read/write/delete access to your files. If you're handling client data, patient records, or anything regulated, you're basically out.The bigger issue is prompt injection. Anthropic admits "the chances of an attack are still non-zero" — and back in October 2025, researchers showed exactly that: a prompt injection against Claude that pulled up to 30MB of user data per request through Anthropic's own API. When you're talking about an agent with file system access, email connectors, and a browser, that's not some theoretical edge case.There's a reason some of us build tools where Claude can search your files without actually touching them. The agentic future is definitely coming, but "AI that can access everything" and "AI that keeps you in control" are two very different products for two very different users.
